author: @voxaris_ai
title_or_hook: Gemini 4 Neon launch: Google's mid-tier model, verified benchmark table
summary: Launch summary for Gemini 4 Neon, Google's new mid-tier flagship-adjacent model, released Nov 18, 2026. The creator's claim that Neon outperforms Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol across several coding, reasoning, and agent tests is TRUE on the aggregate indices and FALSE as a sweep: in DeepMind's own November comparison table Neon leads the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (61 at xhigh vs Opus 59, Sol 57), the Vals Index (70.9% vs 70.1% / 66.1%), and AutomationBench by a wide margin (56.3% vs 42.5% / 41.3%), but LOSES Terminal-Bench 4.1 to Opus (65.2% vs 65.8%), FrontierCode 2.0 to Opus (46.2% vs 47.3%), and Chartography to Sol (73.5% vs 75.1%). Artificial Analysis independently places Neon #3 overall at 61, behind Claude Fable 5.2 (65) and GPT-6.2 Astra (62). API $3 per million input / $0.15 cached / $15 output; 1M-token context; four thinking levels (Low to Extra High). Available in the Gemini app and Antigravity for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, and via the paid Gemini API in AI Studio / Android Studio. Plugs into Garrett's model-routing stack directly: Garrett is on Google AI Ultra (subscribed 2026-11-06), so Neon is already inside a subscription he pays for; no new spend. Harness caveat from DeepMind's own SWE-sweep table: Neon scored 39.0% inside Antigravity vs 12.8% in a shared mini-SWE setup - the harness, not the weights, produced most of the gap. Price trap with a date: Gemini 4 Carbon's introductory $2/$10 rate ends Nov 30, after which Carbon goes to $4/$20 and Neon becomes the cheaper per-token option; any routing comparison written this week expires Dec 1. First test: run one existing fleet bulk task (a sweep-digest class job) on Neon via existing Ultra/Antigravity access and compare output and cost against the current route.

author: @0xsojalsec
summary: A pure-Rust inference engine for Qwen GGUF models - no ggml, no C++ build. Its mechanism for MoE models that exceed VRAM: experts that don't fit run on CPU while the GPU works, with hot experts promoted to GPU; CUDA kernels compile at runtime via NVRTC and the same kernels run on Vulkan. Ships a local chat page, model downloads, and an OpenAI-compatible API server with tool calling, plus a self-tuning calibrate command. v1.2.1 (Nov 8, 2026) supports Qwen3 / Qwen3-Next / Qwen3.5-3.6 hybrids / Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. Plugs into Garrett's model-routing stack / local-model lane - the 'run a big MoE on a 12 GB consumer card' slot; it does not fit this VM (no GPU here), it fits the Windows/Hermes side if a local Qwen lane is ever wanted. The developer-reported headline (up to ~160 tok/s decode with MTP on an RTX 3060 12 GB; roughly 1.3-1.7x llama.cpp across Qwen3 models) is SELF-REPORTED; the independent-looking checks are narrower: 98-99% greedy token agreement with llama.cpp on 20 short prompts, and WikiText-2 perplexity within noise. Risks: solo-developer project, custom license (not a standard OSI license), benchmark comparisons disputed on RAM/tuning/quantization grounds; the downloadable v1.2.1 binary lags the main branch's model list. First test, only if a GPU lane opens: one Qwen3 GGUF, same prompts through RustingStrata and llama.cpp, compare tokens/s and agreement on Garrett's hardware.

author: @0xsojalsec
summary: Evolving Infra (arXiv:2611.12304, submitted Nov 9, 2026) - an open-source LLM serving framework built for agentic workloads, whose irregular patterns break static serving. Mechanism: decouple compute allocation from KV-cache management so any node can switch between prefill and decode roles in ~6.2 s (vs a relaunch in NVIDIA Dynamo), with an online planner setting the prefill/decode split and an agent-aware distributed KV manager that evicts by active-branch counts (fork/spawn/compact/finish signals from the harness) instead of recency. Built on SGLang-derived symmetric engines with a shared host-memory KV pool. Plugs into agent fleet infrastructure as architecture doctrine, not as a deployable for Garrett's current scale (no GPU cluster; their evals ran on 36-256 GB300/H100-class GPUs serving GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6; the harness side must emit branch IDs and lifecycle events). The transferable idea is exact: the branch-aware eviction rule maps onto the fleet's context management today - when an agent compacts or a subagent finishes, evict/re-summarize its zero-branch-count material first, keep live-branch material warm. Reported results are the authors' own evals, independently unreplicated: P95 time-to-first-token up to 14x lower and mean end-to-end latency up to 4.1x lower than Dynamo, 1.10-2.73x throughput. Risks: preprint, author-run benchmarks against one baseline (Dynamo v1.5.1), datacenter hardware; license not read this run. First step: read-and-file - extract the branch-aware eviction policy into the fleet context doctrine; no deploy test.

author: @0xsojalsec
title_or_hook: Agent Substrate, Google's agent orchestrator donated to CNCF
summary: Agent Substrate - a Kubernetes-native runtime for stateful AI agents built on an actor model: agent sessions (Actors) are decoupled from compute (a pre-warmed WorkerPool of sandboxed pods, gVisor isolation by default, optional micro-VM class). Idle agents are snapshotted (memory + files) and restored onto any worker in under 500 ms, giving a claimed 10x density over standard containers and 500+ suspend/resume activations per second - the fix for agents that spend most of their lives waiting on model turns or humans. Reached 1.0; Google donated it (with gVisor and OpenRL) to the CNCF in Sandbox status, announced Nov 5, 2026 at KubeCon NA; GA as a managed capability on GKE, open source for any conformant cluster. How to use: kind-cluster install scripts ship in the repo (hack/create-kind-cluster.sh + install), resources are CRDs under ate.dev/v1alpha1; workloads are standard OCI containers from any framework. Suspension is NOT automatic - the orchestrator must call the suspend API explicitly (a documented caveat). Plugs into agent fleet infrastructure as the scale-out answer if Garrett's fleet ever outgrows single-VM processes: his agents are exactly the mostly-idle, stateful, burst-on-wake shape Substrate is built for, and his standing deployment preference (2026-11-07: on-demand, scale-to-zero, state outside the process) is this system's design statement almost word for word. Today it is oversized for one VM; it is the named candidate the day a cluster exists. Risks: CNCF Sandbox = early governance; maturity signals conflict ('early development, APIs expected to change' language in project material alongside the 1.0/GA announcements), so production-readiness is UNSETTLED; requires real Kubernetes expertise; idle detection is manual. First test if ever needed: kind cluster + the repo's install script + one throwaway actor suspend/resume cycle. Not needed now.
